title: Network Segmentation
summary: A network segment is a bounded group of systems that share a communication policy, and segmentation is the practice of inserting enforced boundaries between those groups so that a single compromised host cannot reach every other asset. Boundaries may be physical, built from separate switches and cabling, logical, built from VLANs with router or firewall access control lists, or identity-based, built from microsegmentation agents and policy engines that decide per workload rather than per subnet. The design goal is to limit blast radius and to create chokepoints where traffic can be inspected and logged. Flat networks fail catastrophically because one phished workstation inherits reachability to file shares, management interfaces, backup infrastructure and directory services. Good segmentation starts from data and service flows rather than from the organisational chart: classify assets by sensitivity, map which systems must talk to which on which ports, then enforce default deny and log the denials until the policy is proven. Segmentation is a programme rather than a purchase. Legacy applications with hard-coded addresses, unmanaged devices, and operational technology that cannot tolerate added latency all generate exceptions that erode the model over time, so each exception needs an owner and an expiry date. Attackers respond by tunnelling permitted protocols, chaining through dual-homed hosts and abusing management planes, which is why monitoring must exist on the boundaries themselves. Administrative tiering, jump hosts and dedicated management networks address the management-plane risk, while cloud security groups, network policies and service meshes reproduce the same ideas with their own drift problems. The practical test of any segmentation scheme is adversarial: assume a host inside a segment is already compromised and ask what it can still reach.
objectives: You will be able to classify assets by sensitivity and derive required communication flows from evidence rather than assumption.
You will be able to design enforced zone boundaries with default deny and documented, expiring exceptions.
You will be able to use flow and firewall logs to detect residual flat-network reachability.
You will be able to describe how administrative tiering and jump hosts reduce management-plane risk.
You will be able to distinguish network, host-based and identity-based microsegmentation and choose appropriately.
You will be able to assess a segmentation design from an assumed-breach perspective and rank the residual paths.
